target.title: fix(context-engine): bound deferred turn maintenance with a per-task timeout (AI-assisted)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A post-turn context-engine **deferred turn maintenance** run can wedge (for example on plugin lock contention) with **no per-task timeout below the ~360s session-level abort**. While it is wedged it holds its maintenance lane, so a user message queued behind it on the same session can wait minutes before being processed, even though the model is healthy. `session.stalled` also re-warns on every ~30s heartbeat with no backoff, spamming the logs.

This matches the report in #96703: an interactive session effectively hangs until a manual stop.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three concrete gaps in core code (independent of any specific context-engine plugin):

1. **No per-task timeout was available on the maintenance enqueue.** `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance` enqueued the maintenance worker via `enqueueCommandInLane(...)` with no options. The command queue already supports a per-task timeout (`taskTimeoutMs` → rejects with `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` and releases the lane), but the maintenance lane never wired it up, so an operator hitting the wedge had no knob below the session-level abort.
2. **A timed-out maintenance worker was not fenced.** Rejecting the enqueue promise releases the lane, but it does not stop the still-running worker. A wedged worker could later call `runtimeContext.rewriteTranscriptEntries()` or complete/fail the task **after** the active run was cleared and a queued foreground turn proceeded, breaking the same-session wait-before-read invariant.
3. **`session.stalled` had no log backoff.** `session.stuck` and `session.long_running` already throttle repeats; `session.stalled` did not.

This change adds the bound + fence mechanism and ships it **opt-in / disabled by default**, so existing deployments whose background maintenance legitimately runs longer than a couple of minutes are not force-cancelled on upgrade. An operator hitting the wedge sets the new key to a positive millisecond value to arm it.

## User Impact

- **No behavior change on upgrade unless configured.** The per-task timeout is **disabled by default** — background turn maintenance keeps running unbounded exactly as before. There is no new force-cancel of long-running background engines on upgrade.
- Operators experiencing the wedge **opt in** by setting `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` to a positive millisecond value (absent or `0` keeps it disabled). When set, a wedged run is bounded at that value and the lane is released, so a queued user message proceeds at ~the timeout instead of waiting for the session-level abort.
- When the bound is armed and fires, late maintenance side effects are **fenced**: the runtime-owned `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper and the worker's terminal complete/fail/descriptor writes become no-ops, so a non-cooperative plugin cannot corrupt session state after the foreground turn has resumed. When the bound is disabled, the fence is never armed.
- A persistently stalled session no longer floods the logs; the first `session.stalled` warning is immediate, repeats are throttled, and recovery is never gated by the backoff.

### Changes

- `command-queue`: add an optional `onTaskTimeout` hook fired synchronously when the per-task timeout rejects, before the lane is released.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: resolve an **opt-in** per-task timeout from `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` (absent / `0` / non-positive ⇒ no bound, no fence); when a positive value is set, pass `taskTimeoutMs` + `onTaskTimeout` to the deferred maintenance enqueue and trip a per-run fence on timeout (hook + defensive trip in the timeout catch); thread the fence into the worker and the runtime-context `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper (checked at entry, inside the session-manager rewrite lock, and before the runtime-transcript write) and before the worker's `completeTaskRunByRunId` / `failTaskRunByRunId` / progress writes.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: scope the timeout classification to the resolved maintenance lane — only this deferred lane's `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` trips the timeout/fence path; a foreign-lane queue timeout surfacing on the enqueue falls through to the normal schedule-failure path (the lane is computed once and reused for enqueue + classification so they cannot drift).
- `session.stalled`: apply the existing `session.stuck`/`session.long_running` warn backoff (`max(last + threshold, last * 2)`), first emission immediate, recovery never gated.
- Config schema accepts `0` (`nonnegative`) as the explicit "disable" sentinel; help/types/docs document the opt-in default.
- New unit coverage: queue `onTaskTimeout` hook; timeout disabled by default and when set to `0`; configured bound + fence arming; late rewrite fenced after timeout; timed-out task not resurrected to succeeded/failed; checkpoint-after-timeout ordering; `session.stalled` backoff.

## Evidence

AI-assisted PR (implemented with an AI coding agent; author reviewed and understands the change).

**Static / unit validation** (this branch):
- `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:test:src` — clean
- `command-queue.test.ts` — 34 passed; `context-engine-maintenance.test.ts` — 60 passed (incl. disabled-by-default, `0`-disables, and fence cases)
- `oxfmt --check` + oxlint on touched files — clean
- `CHANGELOG.md` not touched (left for maintainers at landing)

**Real runtime reproduction (end-to-end, in a container).** A real gateway was started in a container running this branch, with a real context-engine plugin selected via `plugins.slots.contextEngine` whose `info.turnMaintenanceMode = "background"` (so a normal `reason:"turn"` run is deferred through `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance`). Its `maintain()` deliberately sleeps 12s (longer than the configured timeout) and then attempts a late transcript rewrite. The bound was **explicitly opted in** for the test: `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs = 5000`. Two real agent turns were run on one session. Everything in the queue/timeout/fence/transcript-rewrite path is real production code; only the plugin's deliberate sleep is contrived. Logs redacted (provider/model/host/ids replaced with placeholders):

```
[T+0.00s] [context-engine] deferred turn maintenance queued taskId=<id-1> sessionKey=<session> lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session>
[T+0.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 START                       # deferred maintenance begins, will sleep 12s
[T+2.87s] (queued) second turn is waiting behind the in-flight deferred maintenance on the session lane
[T+5.00s] [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session> durationMs=5000 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: ... task timed out after 5000ms"
[T+5.00s] [agent/embedded] deferred context engine maintenance timed out: sessionKey=<session> taskId=<id-1> taskTimeoutMs=5000
[T+5.06s] [agent/embedded] embedded run start: <turn-2>   # queued turn RELEASED at the 5s timeout — NOT after the 12s wedge, NOT after the ~360s session abort
[T+12.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 WOKE after 12000ms sleep, attempting late rewrite   # the wedged worker finally wakes, 7s after the lane was released
[T+12.01s] [wedge] maintain#1 late rewrite result: {"changed":false,"bytesFreed":0,"rewrittenEntries":0,"reason":"maintenance fenced after timeout"}   # FENCED -> no-op
```

Fence scope is correct: the second turn's **foreground** maintenance (not timed out) is **not** fenced (`reason: "no replacements requested"`); only the timed-out **deferred** runs are fenced. With the bound left at its default (disabled), neither the timeout nor the fence arms and background maintenance runs unbounded as before. A scripted reproduction is available on request.

Closes #96703

target.title: fix(infra): validate callTool arguments against declared inputSchema
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

MCP stdio servers that expose OpenClaw plugin tools (`plugin-tools-serve`, `openclaw-tools-serve`) advertise an `inputSchema` for each tool but do not validate arguments against it before execution. Clients sending malformed arguments get cryptic internal errors rather than clear validation failures, breaking the MCP contract.

## Why This Change Was Made

`createPluginToolsMcpHandlers` in `plugin-tools-handlers.ts` passes `params.arguments ?? {}` directly to `tool.execute()` without checking the tool's parameter schema. The schema is already resolved for `listTools` but is unused in `callTool`.

The fix pre-compiles a TypeBox `Compile` Validator for each tool and calls `validator.Check(args)` before execution. On failure, `[...validator.Errors(args)]` produces structured multi-error messages returned via the MCP `isError` envelope.

This replaces the earlier `validateToolArgs` approach (which only checked `required` + `additionalProperties`) with the canonical full JSON Schema validator from TypeBox 1.3.3, covering type constraints, nested objects, enums, min/max, pattern, and all other JSON Schema keywords.

## User Impact

- MCP clients (Claude Desktop, ACP hosts, IDEs) calling plugin tools with missing required properties now receive a clear `isError: true` response:
  `Invalid arguments for tool "greet": must have required properties name`
- Type mismatches report the path and expected type:
  `Invalid arguments for tool "math_add": a: must be integer; b: must be integer`
- Unexpected properties are rejected when `additionalProperties: false` is declared:
  `Invalid arguments for tool "strict_greet": must not have additional properties`
- No impact on valid tool calls — validation is purely additive and schema-defined
- Existing MCP clients are not affected: `additionalProperties` defaults to `true` per JSON Schema spec, so only tools that explicitly declare constraints are enforced

## Evidence

### Transcript (direct handler invocation — same code path as MCP stdio server)

```
================================================================
  MCP callTool Validation — Live Proof
  PR #109148 — Compile-based full JSON Schema validation
================================================================

Step 1: listTools
  Tool:  greet
  inputSchema: {"type":"object","properties":{"name":{"type":"string"}},"required":["name"]}
  Tool:  math_add
  inputSchema: {"type":"object","properties":{"a":{"type":"integer"},"b":{"type":"integer"}},"required":["a","b"]}
  Tool:  strict_greet
  inputSchema: {"type":"object","properties":{"name":{"type":"string"}},"required":["name"],"additionalProperties":false}
  Tool:  noop
  inputSchema: {"type":"object","properties":{}}

Step 2: VALID arguments
  isError=undefined  content=[{"type":"text","text":"done: greet"}]
  → execute() was called — tool runs normally

Step 3: MISSING required property
  isError=true  content=[{"type":"text","text":"Invalid arguments for tool "greet": must have required properties name"}]
  → execute() was NOT called — blocked by validator

Step 4: TYPE MISMATCH
  isError=true  content=[{"type":"text","text":"Invalid arguments for tool "math_add": a: must be integer; b: must be integer"}]
  → execute() was NOT called — type constraints enforced

Step 5: UNEXPECTED property (additionalProperties:false)
  isError=true  content=[{"type":"text","text":"Invalid arguments for tool "strict_greet": must not have additional properties"}]
  → execute() was NOT called — extra property rejected

Step 6: No-constraint tool
  isError=undefined  content=[{"type":"text","text":"done: noop"}]
  → execute() was called — empty schema accepts anything

Step 7: UNKNOWN tool
  isError=true  content=[{"type":"text","text":"Unknown tool: nonexistent"}]
  → Unknown-tool error (unchanged)

Step 8: EXECUTION error
  isError=true  content=[{"type":"text","text":"Tool error: internal failure"}]
  → Execution error still reported correctly
```

### Real MCP stdio integration transcript

Proof harness: `StdioClientTransport` (stdin/stdout pipes) → MCP `Server` → `createPluginToolsMcpHandlers`. This exercises the full MCP JSON-RPC protocol through real stdio transport, not just direct handler invocation.

```
================================================================
  MCP callTool Validation — Real MCP Stdio Proof
  PR #109148 — Compile-based full JSON Schema validation
================================================================

Connecting to MCP stdio server...
  → connected

listTools
  Tool:  greet
  inputSchema: {"type":"object","properties":{"name":{"type":"string"}},"required":["name"]}
  Tool:  math_add
  inputSchema: {"type":"object","properties":{"a":{"type":"integer"},"b":{"type":"integer"}},"required":["a","b"]}

VALID callTool: greet with { name: "Alice" }
  isError=undefined  content=[{"type":"text","text":"Hello, Alice!"}]
  → execute() was called — tool runs normally

INVALID callTool: greet with {} (missing required 'name')
  isError=true  content=[{"type":"text","text":"Invalid arguments for tool "greet": must have required properties name"}]
  → execute() was NOT called — blocked by validator

INVALID callTool: math_add with { a: 'x', b: 'y' } (wrong types)
  isError=true  content=[{"type":"text","text":"Invalid arguments for tool "math_add": a: must be integer; b: must be integer"}]
  → execute() was NOT called — type constraints enforced

INVALID callTool: unknown tool name
  isError=true  content=[{"type":"text","text":"Unknown tool: nonexistent"}]
  → Unknown-tool error (unchanged from before fix)
```

### Test results

- `pnpm test src/mcp/`: **115 tests passed** across 14 test files
- `check-test-types`: **passed** — fixed the content union `.text` access by narrowing before reading
- New regression tests (8 cases): missing required properties, type constraints, additionalProperties rejection, valid args pass-through, nested object validation, enum violations, multi-constraint violations, no-constraint tool pass-through
- All existing validation behavior (unknown tool, execution errors) preserved

target.title: feat(gateway): pre-handshake WS verifyClient with Sec-Fetch-Site and forwarded-header hardening
target.body:
# PR Title

`feat(gateway): pre-handshake WS verifyClient with Sec-Fetch-Site and forwarded-header hardening`

---

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw's gateway already validates browser `Origin` on the WebSocket path, but only **post-handshake** (in `src/gateway/server/ws-connection/connect-admission.ts`, after the socket is already open), and it does **not** defend against:

- **Header-smuggling / contradiction attacks** — a client forging `X-Forwarded-For` to disagree with `Forwarded` (or vice-versa) to confuse the resolved client IP / trust decision.
- **Cross-site WebSocket initiations (CSRF / DNS-rebinding class)** — there is no `Sec-Fetch-Site` gate anywhere in `main` (`git grep` confirms zero `sec-fetch-site` enforcement in `src/`).
- **Proto contradiction** — `X-Forwarded-Proto` / `Forwarded proto` disagreeing with the actual socket transport (without breaking legitimate TLS-terminating trusted proxies).

These gaps are the WebSocket sibling of the now-closed HTTP ingress CSRF findings **#102834** and **#96486**, and sit *under* the origin-allowlist work in **#98924** (which decides *which* origins pass, not *when/how the gate runs*).

This PR adds a self-contained **pre-handshake** `verifyClient` gate attached to the gateway `WebSocketServer({ noServer: true })`, so unauthenticated or forged clients never complete the HTTP 101 upgrade.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Pre-handshake beats post-handshake.** Running the checks in `verifyClient` (before the 101) means a rejected client never gets a live socket, matching the defense-in-depth posture maintainers expect for a network-exposed gateway.
- **Reuses the shared `checkBrowserOrigin`** rather than reinventing origin logic, so allowlist / same-host / loopback behavior stays consistent with the HTTP/WS admission paths.
- **All strictness is opt-in and default-off** (`gateway.security.strictHeaderValidation`, `rejectUntrustedProxyHeaders`, `rejectCrossSiteWebSocketRequests`), so existing deployments have **zero behavior change**. Non-browser clients (CLI, native apps) send no `Origin` and pass through; they authenticate post-handshake as today.
- **Trusted proxies are correctly exempted** from the proto-mismatch check — a TLS-terminating proxy legitimately presents plaintext to the gateway.

This is complementary to **#98924** (`allowedOriginPatterns`): that PR extends *which* loopback origins are allowed; this PR adds the *enforcement layer* (pre-handshake gate, header contradiction, `Sec-Fetch-Site`). Neither duplicates the other.

## Prior Attempt & What Improved

This is a follow-up to my earlier (closed) PR **#35109** (`fix(gateway): surgical proxy-aware origin validation`), which edited the shared `checkBrowserOrigin` on the *post-handshake* WS path. Compared to that attempt, this PR:

- Moves the gate to **pre-handshake** (`verifyClient` before the 101) instead of extending the post-handshake check — a rejected client never opens a socket.
- Adds the **`Sec-Fetch-Site` cross-site rejection** and **`X-Forwarded-For` vs `Forwarded` IP-contradiction** checks that #35109 did not cover.
- Keeps the change **self-contained** in `verify-client.ts` + `forwarded-headers.ts` rather than widening the shared `checkBrowserOrigin` contract used by every HTTP/WS caller.
- Ran the `autoreview` closeout gate before opening; it caught a real **`Origin: null` bypass** (a literal `null` origin was treated like an absent header and skipped all browser validation). Fixed in `verify-client.ts` with a regression test — the gate now only fast-passes on a *truly absent* Origin.

The goal was to take the earlier direction, make it architecturally cleaner, and actually vet it before asking for review.

## User Impact

- Network-exposed gateways gain a pre-handshake defense against forged forwarded headers and cross-site WebSocket CSRF, with **no config change required** for existing users (all new behavior opt-in).
- Operators who want stricter posture can enable:
  - `gateway.security.strictHeaderValidation` — reject duplicate / comma-chained sensitive proxy headers.
  - `gateway.security.rejectUntrustedProxyHeaders` — reject proxy headers from non-trusted peers.
  - `gateway.security.rejectCrossSiteWebSocketRequests` — reject `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` / `cross-origin` WebSocket upgrades. **Off by default**; opt in only when every legitimate browser WS client is same-origin to the gateway. Loopback aliases (e.g. `localhost` -> `127.0.0.1`) are legitimately flagged cross-site by browsers, so the gate stays opt-in and `checkBrowserOrigin` remains authoritative.

## Evidence

Real gateway/WS behavior, driven through the actual `verify-client` factory (not mocked):

```
# Trusted proxy presenting plaintext X-Forwarded-Proto -> ACCEPTED (proto-mismatch exempt)
remote=127.0.0.1  origin=https://app.example.com  x-forwarded-proto=https  -> ok=true

# Identical request from an UNTRUSTED peer -> REJECTED
remote=198.51.100.7  origin=https://app.example.com  x-forwarded-proto=https  -> ok=false

# Cross-site WebSocket initiation from a browser -> REJECTED (Sec-Fetch-Site)
remote=192.0.2.10  origin=https://evil.example.com  sec-fetch-site=cross-site -> ok=false

# Literal "null" browser origin -> REJECTED (no longer skips the gate)
remote=192.0.2.10  origin=null  sec-fetch-site=cross-site -> ok=false

# Non-browser client with no Origin header -> PASSES THROUGH
remote=192.0.2.10  (no Origin)  -> ok=true
```

- Test file: `src/gateway/server/verify-client.test.ts` — **5/5 passing** (trusted-proxy wiring regression, untrusted-peer reject, cross-site reject, `Origin: null` reject, non-browser pass-through). The trusted-proxy case guards a real prior regression where `gateway.trustedProxies` was never read at the call site.
- `tsgo` typecheck: **clean** on both `verify-client.ts` and `forwarded-headers.ts`.
- `autoreview` (Codex, high reasoning): initially reported the `Origin: null` bypass; after the fix, no accepted/actionable findings.

## Scope / Out of scope

- **In scope:** `src/gateway/server/verify-client.ts` (new, wired at `server-runtime-state.ts`), `src/gateway/forwarded-headers.ts` (validators), their tests, and the `gateway.security.*` config surface in `src/config/types.gateway.ts` + `src/config/zod-schema.ts`.
- **Out of scope (left to maintainer decision):** the `#98924` allowlist-wildcard contract, and the broader `gateway.browserOrigins` client/role-scoped policy direction.
- **`Sec-Fetch-Site` note for reviewers:** upstream deliberately avoids a blanket `cross-site` reject on MCP **HTTP** because browsers flag legit local MCP as cross-site. This PR mirrors that posture for the **WebSocket upgrade** path: the reject is **opt-in** (`gateway.security.rejectCrossSiteWebSocketRequests: true`) and runs *after* `checkBrowserOrigin`, so the existing origin allowlist / loopback-alias admission (shipped in v2026.4.15, PR #66665) remains authoritative. Native/CLI clients send no `Sec-Fetch-Site` header so they pass through regardless.

## Related

- Sibling enforcement: **#98924** (`allowedOriginPatterns`, open) — which origins are allowed.
- Prior art (closed security findings this complements): **#102834** (HTTP ingress CSRF under `auth.mode=none`), **#96486** (CSRF via the existing `gateway.controlUi.dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback`, which this PR reuses verbatim rather than duplicating).
- Prior attempt by me: **#35109** (closed) — see "Prior Attempt & What Improved".

cc @steipete — this sits on the gateway origin/security boundary you own (and is the sibling of #98924 / the closed #102834, #96486). The `Sec-Fetch-Site` reject is scoped to the WS upgrade pre-handshake specifically because of the MCP-HTTP caveat you handled; happy to align flag names / gate position with #98924 before merge if you'd prefer.


---

## ClawSweeper Follow-up (head `1b5c1de`)

Addressed all four findings from the July 17 ClawSweeper review in a single follow-up commit (`1b5c1de7ed5`):

1. **[P1] Default-on Sec-Fetch-Site reject → opt-in.** `rejectCrossSiteWebSocketRequests` now defaults to `false` (`=== true` instead of `!== false`), matching this PR's stated "all flags default-off" design and preserving the v2026.4.15 / PR #66665 loopback-alias contract that browsers legitimately flag as `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site`. Regression test added (`allows legitimate loopback cross-site traffic by default`).
2. **[P1] Duplicate config field removed.** `gateway.security.dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback` is gone; `verify-client` now reads the existing `gateway.controlUi.dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback` so pre-handshake and post-handshake admission share one source of truth.
3. **[P2] Canonical IPv6 parsing.** `forwarded-headers.ts` now uses `normalizeIpAddress` from `@openclaw/net-policy/ip` instead of `split(":")[0]`. Bracketed / unbracketed / port-suffixed IPv6 literals all normalize correctly. Regression tests added for IPv6 contradiction detection and matching-across-forms.
4. **[P2] Public config contract completed.** `gateway.security` plus its three leaf fields now have entries in `schema.labels.ts`, `schema.tags.ts`, and `schema.help.ts` (all ≥80 chars with operational guidance, per `schema.help.quality.test.ts`).

Net diff: +50/-40 prod LOC across 8 files. The PR got smaller, not larger. All unit tests (`verify-client`: 8/8, `schema.help.quality`: 22/22) and `tsgo` core typecheck are green on the new head.

target.title: feat(zalouser): surface inbound photo attachments via media array
target.body:
## Summary

Surfaces inbound photo attachments on the Zalo personal-account channel as native vision content blocks. Previously the `zalouser` monitor handler dropped Zalo photo metadata, so agents only saw the user's text caption and could not respond to image content. After this PR an inbound Zalo photo lands on the agent's turn as a kernel vision block, and the model can reason about the image directly.

## What changes

- `extensions/zalouser/src/zalo-js.ts`: new `extractInboundMedia(content)` helper that recognises photo content payloads from `zca-js` events. Detects via `type === 'photo'`, image-extension URL pattern, or non-empty `thumb`. Returns `{ kind: 'image', url, thumbUrl? }` for downstream pickup.
- `extensions/zalouser/src/zalo-js.ts`: `toInboundMessage` returns a new `media` field populated from `extractInboundMedia`.
- `extensions/zalouser/src/monitor.ts`: new `resolveInboundImageContentType(detected, url)` helper that trusts a real `image/*` MIME when the CDN returns one, otherwise maps the URL extension (`.jpg|.png|.gif|.webp|.bmp`) to the correct image MIME. Falls back to `image/jpeg` when both signals are absent. Closes the Zalo-CDN-returns-`application/octet-stream` bug where the kernel rejected the photo because `MediaType` did not start with `image/`.
- `extensions/zalouser/src/monitor.ts`: when an inbound message carries a `media` payload, fetch the photo (via existing `saveRemoteMedia` plumbing), persist to the agent volume, and wire `{ path, url, contentType }` into the `core.channel.turn.buildContext({ media: [...] })` call. The kernel auto-derives `MediaPath/MediaUrl/MediaType` so the photo reaches the model as a native vision block.
- `extensions/zalouser/src/monitor.ts`: relax the empty-body guard so a photo-only message (zero text content) is not dropped.

## Tests

- `extensions/zalouser/src/monitor.media.test.ts` - new test file for `resolveInboundImageContentType` with 7 cases covering happy-path image/* trust, Zalo CDN `application/octet-stream` override, URL extension fallback, case-insensitivity, query-string stripping, unknown extensions, and the missing-both fallback to `image/jpeg`.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Inbound Zalo photo attachments arriving via the `@openclaw/zalouser` channel were silently dropped by `monitor.ts` - the model saw only the user's text caption, never the image. Two compounding bugs: (1) `toInboundMessage` did not surface the photo content at all, (2) the Zalo CDN returns `Content-Type: application/octet-stream` for photos, so even when fetched the kernel's `resolveCurrentTurnImages` rejected the file because `MediaType` did not start with `image/`.

**Real environment tested**: Em Huyen agent (Tingee customer-support bot, Vietnamese) running on the openclaw runtime with `@openclaw/zalouser` paired to a real Zalo personal account, talking to a real Zalo group room (Capypara.AI). Channel `zalouser`, model `dos-ai/dos-ai` (Qwen3.6-35B-a3b). Tested on both Zalo Mobile (Android) and Zalo Desktop on the same conversation.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
1. Apply this PR's `zalo-js.ts` + `monitor.ts` changes to the running zalouser plugin.
2. Restart the agent container so the plugin reloads.
3. From a separate Zalo account, send a photo of a Tingee soundbox bottom plate to the Capypara.AI group with the text `@Em Huyền reset loa cho anh`. The plate has a printed sticker showing `Model: Tingee 3PRO`, `SN: 3PRO175459`.
4. Wait for Em Huyen to reply.
5. Open the same conversation on Zalo Android and on Zalo Desktop; screenshot the inbound photo + bot reply.

**Evidence after fix**:

Zalo Android (Capypara.AI group, dark theme):

![Em Huyen extracts SN from inbound photo on Zalo Android](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JOY/openclaw/proof/zalouser-em-huyen-screenshots/docs/proof/zalouser-em-huyen/zalo-mobile.jpg)

Zalo Desktop (same conversation):

![Em Huyen extracts SN from inbound photo on Zalo Desktop](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JOY/openclaw/proof/zalouser-em-huyen-screenshots/docs/proof/zalouser-em-huyen/zalo-desktop.jpg)

**Observed result after fix**: Em Huyen's reply opens with `Dạ anh Le, em đã nhìn rõ ảnh rồi. Mã thiết bị của anh là: SN: 3PRO175459 (Model: Tingee 3PRO).` That SN string is printed on the physical label in the photo - the agent extracted it directly from the inbound vision block, not from prior context. Confirms end-to-end that (a) `extractInboundMedia` recognised the Zalo photo content payload, (b) `resolveInboundImageContentType` overrode the Zalo CDN's `application/octet-stream` to `image/jpeg`, (c) the kernel vision pipeline accepted the photo, (d) the agent received the image as a native vision block and read the SN off the label.

**What was not tested**: I have not run a head-to-head BEFORE / AFTER screenshot pair in the same Zalo conversation - the pre-fix behavior was the live deployment state captured separately in the downstream vendor patch's tracking ticket, which is what motivated this PR. The AFTER screenshots above are from a real deployment with the fix in place. Maintainers can reproduce the BEFORE state by reverting `extensions/zalouser/src/monitor.ts` to the pre-PR version and re-sending the same photo - the bot will reply without referencing the SN because it never received the vision block.

Screenshots live on a separate `proof/zalouser-em-huyen-screenshots` branch on the fork so the upstream merge does not import binaries into openclaw history.

## Refs

Companion outbound PR: openclaw/openclaw#85039 (Zalo client markdown normalizer).

target.title: fix(ui): restore first-run setup redirect after reconnect
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where first-time Control UI users could remain on an unconfigured chat screen after `openclaw.setup.detect` failed during a transient Gateway disconnect. The first-run redirect recorded the failed request as its only attempt, so a replacement Gateway client was never checked.

## Why This Change Was Made

The redirect now scopes detection attempts to the Gateway client that owns them. A replacement client can retry immediately, a failed current-client attempt becomes retryable, and a late result from an obsolete client cannot redirect the current page.

## User Impact

Fresh users who reconnect while the initial setup check is failing are guided to Model Setup without reloading the Control UI. Successful connections still perform only one detection request and redirect at most once.

## Evidence

- **Behavior addressed:** A failed first-run setup detection no longer permanently suppresses setup guidance after Gateway reconnection.
- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64, Node 24.15.0, commit `437b8c2f` on branch `fix/model-setup-first-run-reconnect`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `node --import tsx /tmp/verify-model-setup-first-run.mts` drives the real first-run redirect module through a rejected client request followed by a replacement client.
- **Evidence after fix:** Terminal capture of `node` runtime verification (live stdout):

  ```text
  PASS first=1 replacement=1 redirects=1
  ```

- **Observed result after fix:** The failed client was attempted once, the replacement client was attempted once, and setup navigation occurred exactly once.
- **What was not tested:** A visual browser recording against a deliberately interrupted live Gateway was not captured; the focused DOM-independent runtime path and UI unit suite cover the connection transition deterministically.

## Tests and validation

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/model-setup/first-run.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       5 passed (5)

$ git diff upstream/main...HEAD --check
EXIT=0
```

The new regression test failed on the pre-fix implementation because the replacement client received zero requests, then passed after the client-scoped lifecycle change.

## Risk checklist

- User-visible behavior: Yes - first-run setup guidance retries after reconnect.
- Config/env/migration behavior: No - no persisted state or configuration changes.
- Security/auth/secrets/network/tool execution: No - existing admin-scope and advertised-method gates are unchanged.
- Plugins/providers/channels/SDK: No - Control UI-only lifecycle handling.
- Highest-risk area: Duplicate setup detection during repeated Gateway snapshots.
- Mitigation: Attempts remain deduplicated per client, and existing one-request/one-redirect coverage remains green.

target.title: fix(line): replies vanish when claim refresh races turn adoption
target.body:
Closes #109931

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a LINE user's reply silently vanishes when the spool's claim-refresh fence races the turn-adoption completion write. A refresh tick that observes the just-completed row (or throws while the completion persist is in flight) aborts the delivery even though the turn is already durably adopted; the ingress row finishes `completed`, so nothing retries or redelivers - the message is consumed and the user never gets a response.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fence's abort path checks `!adopted`, but `adopted` is only set after the completion write commits, so the fence can outlive the start of adoption. The fix stops the refresh fence as the first synchronous statement of `onTurnAdopted`, before the completion write: from the moment adoption begins committing, the abort path is structurally unreachable (both callback branches check the `refreshing` flag), closing the refresh-false microtask window and the wider refresh-error window in one move. Setting `adopted = true` before the write instead was rejected because a completion write that then loses the claim-token fence would be misreported as completed and invite duplicate delivery. Keeping the fence refreshing through the write behind a "completing" flag (the core drain's wedged-over-duplicated lease philosophy) was also rejected: lease refreshes are writes to the same store, so in the store-failure scenario where the completion write actually wedges, refresh cannot keep the lease fresh either - it adds state for no real-scenario gain. The fence's pre-adoption job - aborting a delivery whose claim another owner genuinely reclaimed - is untouched. The core drain guards this same class on its side by swallowing refresh errors and no-oping lease-reclaim marking once settled (`src/channels/message/ingress-drain.ts:240-253`, `:275`).

## User Impact

Replies no longer disappear when a refresh tick lands in the adoption window or a store hiccup makes a refresh throw during the completion persist. Genuine ownership loss during the completion write still surfaces (the write's own claim-token fence returns false), and deliveries whose claim is reclaimed before adoption are still aborted and released for retry, exactly as before.

## Evidence

Behavior addressed: the claim-refresh fence aborts an already-adopting delivery; the row completes and the reply is lost with no retry.

Real environment tested: real SQLite ingress queue (`createChannelIngressQueueForTests`) driven through the exported `createLineWebhookSpool` factory; the race window is widened deterministically (completion write slowed to 100ms, refresh cadence 5ms, `refreshClaim` returning `false` once the write starts); Windows 11, Node 24.15.0.

Before evidence (current main): the delivery's `abortSignal` fires after `onTurnAdopted` resolves - the new regression test fails in ~0.4s:

```
Test Files  1 failed (1)
  x does not abort an adopting delivery when claim refresh races the completion write
```

Evidence after fix (same harness, only the fence ordering changed):

```
Tests  3 passed | 14 skipped (17)   <- targeted run, single execution:
  - does not abort an adopting delivery when claim refresh races the completion write
  - completes at durable turn adoption without replaying later failures
  - aborts delivery and releases the row when claim refresh loses ownership   <- fence's pre-adoption job intact
```

Observed result after fix: the adopting delivery is never aborted, the outcome settles `completed`, and both neighbouring semantics (durable-adoption completion, pre-adoption ownership-loss abort) hold unchanged.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```
pnpm exec vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-line.config.ts extensions/line/src/webhook-spool.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1) / Tests  17 passed (17)
```

Control-red: reverting the source reorder makes the new test fail (delivery aborted after adoption) while all sixteen existing tests still pass, so the suite pins the new invariant without disturbing any pinned behavior.

Additional review: extension source typecheck (`tsconfig.extensions.json`), extension test-types typecheck (`test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json`), `pnpm lint:extensions`, and `oxfmt --check` on touched files all pass; the branch is rebased onto current main.

What was not tested: no live LINE-platform run - the race is a sub-second interleaving of two internal callbacks that cannot be choreographed from the platform side; the deterministic harness that widens the window is the instrument that can actually exercise it, in line with the copied-output criterion applied to the sibling lifecycle fix in #109898's review.

Proof limitations or environment constraints: Windows 11 local runs; the widened-window timings (100ms/5ms/50ms) are harness parameters, not production tunables.

target.title: feat(discord): show subagent progress
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Discord users can see a parent turn as idle while tracked subagents are still running. The source message provides no compact indication of concurrent child work or terminal failure.

## Why This Change Was Made

Core now emits one generic typed `subagent_progress` presentation event with source-message provenance. The Discord plugin maps that portable event to typing plus one count reaction, and retains a red reaction after a non-OK child outcome. One opt-in switch, `channels.discord.subagentProgress`, controls the behavior; emoji, cadence, and the one-hour typing bound remain internal defaults.

The maintainer rewrite deliberately keeps transport policy in Discord, routes native and tracked ACP spawns through the same core lifecycle, and persists only Discord reaction ownership and terminal outcome in plugin SQLite. Durable rows make count cleanup and failure presentation retry-safe across response loss and gateway restart without blocking subagent lifecycle delivery. Progress runtime code remains behind its own lazy import so the public Discord API and unrelated subagent hooks do not increase lightweight CLI startup memory.

## User Impact

When enabled, the Discord source message shows `1️⃣` through `🔟` as tracked child concurrency changes, removes the count after the final child ends, keeps typing active for up to one hour, and leaves `🔴` for error, timeout, or killed outcomes. Other channels ignore the generic event and keep current behavior.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/subagent-hooks.test.ts extensions/discord/src/subagent-progress.test.ts src/agents/subagent-registry.persistence.test.ts src/plugins/wired-hooks-subagent.test.ts` — 90 passed across three shards.
- `node --max-old-space-size=8192 --import tsx scripts/generate-plugin-sdk-api-baseline.ts --check` — baseline current.
- `git diff --check` — clean.
- Fresh whole-branch and final-patch autoreviews — no accepted/actionable findings.
- [Blacksmith changed-surface gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29572285337) — green: format, SDK baseline, plugin boundaries, extension production and test typechecks, extension lint, database-first, runtime sidecar, import-cycle, and related guards.
- Contributor live Discord proof already recorded on this PR covered count add/replace/remove, concurrent children, channel/thread sources, typing drain, and a retained failure reaction. The rewrite preserves that user-visible shape while replacing the original configurable/internal hook design with the approved generic event and one-toggle contract.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #29707. Amazon Nova generation models on Bedrock were still treated as unsupported non-Anthropic models, so OpenClaw forced `cacheRetention: "none"` and never emitted Bedrock `cachePoint` blocks for Nova requests.

## Why This Change Was Made

AWS documents explicit prompt caching support for Amazon Bedrock models, including Nova generation models: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html

This change teaches the Bedrock provider to recognize Nova Micro, Lite, Pro, Premier, and Nova 2 Lite refs, lets direct Nova requests keep their explicit cache settings, and keeps the existing no-cache fallback for unsupported non-Anthropic Bedrock models. For Nova, `cacheRetention: "long"` emits the default Bedrock cache point without reusing Claude's `ttl: "1h"` field.

Nova eligibility now has a single owner: the Amazon Bedrock provider normalization seam. The provider sets generic runtime compatibility metadata for eligible Nova models, while the shared agent cache-retention path only consumes that capability and contains no Bedrock model IDs or Nova-family matcher.

## User Impact

Users can enable prompt caching for Bedrock Nova text models without hitting the previous runtime no-cache override. Unsupported non-Anthropic Bedrock models, such as Mistral, continue to be protected from unsupported cache metadata.

target.title: fix: compaction usage guards and agent-loop turn correctness
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a cluster of agent-loop and compaction correctness bugs:

- A stream that dies before its terminal usage event persists all-zero usage; that anchors the context-size estimate near zero, threshold auto-compaction silently stops firing, and later requests die on context overflow.
- Tool results without `content` inject `undefined` into the transcript and crash provider conversion on the next request, aborting the run with a malformed message persisted.
- Compaction budgets skipped context-visible entries (plugin-injected messages, branch summaries), so the keep-recent window was computed against the wrong token totals and cut points could not land on those boundaries.
- Compaction could produce empty summary entries when there was nothing to summarize.
- A *successful* response with high token usage could be misclassified as silent overflow, popping the completed assistant message and burning the one-shot overflow-recovery flag.
- A threshold compaction that ran just before delivering a queued user prompt resumed the loop first, so the model answered the compaction summary unprompted.
- Follow-ups queued by handlers reacting to the run ending were never delivered.
- Mid-run system-prompt/tool/model changes did not apply to the next turn on the session path (the wrapper dropped the loop's per-turn refresh context). This is now an explicit `AgentOptions.prepareNextTurnWithContext` API (additive; baseline regenerated via the sanctioned workflow).
- `dispose()` left retry/compaction/branch-summary/bash/agent work running.
- Settings reload did not resync steering/follow-up queue modes; after-tool-call overrides dropped unknown result fields.

## Why This Change Was Made

These bugs compound in long sessions: broken usage accounting disables compaction exactly when it is most needed, and the loop-state gaps surface as duplicated or lost messages. The cut-point/turn-boundary logic is now expressed through one projection helper instead of parallel entry-type switches.

## User Impact

Long sessions keep compacting reliably; runs no longer crash on content-less tool results; queued messages are neither answered out of order nor dropped; mid-run model/prompt/tool changes take effect on the next turn; disposal is clean.

## Evidence

- 56 focused tests passing across `packages/agent-core` (agent-loop, compaction) and `src/agents/sessions` (context-usage, new loop-correctness suite with 10 cases), re-run after rebase onto current `main`.
- `pnpm plugin-sdk:api:check` and `pnpm plugin-sdk:surface:check` green (350 entrypoints; additive API only).
- Core + core-test typechecks and changed-file lint green (hosted run 29558685534).


**Live verification (real API keys):** `node scripts/test-live.mjs -- src/agents/sessions/agent-session.live.test.ts` — 3/3 against a real Claude model: a full agent turn with a registered tool executing end-to-end, **manual compaction of a small real session** (this PR's zero-retention replan producing a real model-generated summary, with the session remaining usable), and queued follow-up drain delivering a second answered message. Live suite added in this PR (gated on `OPENCLAW_LIVE_TEST=1` + key).

target.title: perf(ci): collapse remaining per-PR sticky-disk minters to O(1) keys
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Blacksmith installation is at its 1000-backing-disk cap and every sticky mount currently 429s fleet-wide — the reason the landed warm-path levers (#109752 node-deps, #109804 ext-boundary) cannot produce a single warm hit. The cap was reached because sticky keys embedded PR numbers and content hashes, minting a new disk per PR and per input change. Two minters remained after the earlier re-keys.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Vitest fs transform cache**: `vitest-fs-v2-<pr-N|protected>-…` collapses to the one existing protected disk. Cache entries are content-hash keyed (sha1 over id+content+NODE_ENV+version+config), so cross-PR sharing is safe by construction — PRs now mount the protected snapshot read-only (`commit: "false"`), the separate PR-only seed mount is deleted, and writers (non-PR shard writer + scheduled warm run) keep explicit `commit: true`. The PR-close cleanup workflow (`pr-cache-cleanup.yml`) is deleted with the per-PR disks it existed to reap. Trade-off named: a PR loses warm entries only for files it changed itself, which re-transform once per push either way. Disk count: 1 + O(open PRs) → 1.
- **Gradle**: `gradle-v1-<task>-<pr-N|hashFiles>` → `gradle-v2-<task>`. Task scope stays (a light ktlint lane must not seed the heavy build lanes); the dependency hash moves into an in-job fingerprint marker that makes the non-PR writer rebuild cold on input changes; PR mounts are read-only and safely reuse stale snapshots because Gradle caches are content-addressed. Disk count: O(tasks × PRs × dependency bumps) → O(tasks), 7 today.
- **Docker builder**: audited out of scope — `useblacksmith/setup-docker-builder` keys internally by repo name only (`src/setup_builder.ts` `getStickyDisk`) and cannot mint per-PR disks.
- Guards updated: no sticky key may reference `github.event.pull_request.number` or `hashFiles()`, single-writer/read-only invariants pinned, and a stays-deleted check replaces the cleanup-workflow assertions.

## User Impact

None at runtime — CI-only. This stops the disk-cap regrowth so the operator purge is durable; combined with the purge it unlocks the warm paths of every sticky lever.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/ci-workflow-guards.test.ts` — 80 passed, 1 skipped (rerun green after rebase onto current main).
- `pnpm check:test-types` clean; `actionlint` clean; `git diff --check` clean.
- Disk-count math per surface in the commit body; docker-builder audit cites the action source.

target.title: feat(feishu): bot-to-bot conversation support with @mention handling
target.body:
## Summary

Adds a bounded, default-off Feishu bot-to-bot ingress path.

- `channels.feishu.allowBots: true` (or the account-scoped equivalent) opts an account into bot-authored group messages. Omitted/false remains disabled.
- Bot-authored events are accepted only when the receiving bot is actually mentioned. Same-app mention IDs are checked directly; cross-app-scoped IDs are verified by re-reading the message with the receiving app token.
- Self-authored, unmentioned, unrelated, or unverifiable bot events fail closed before authorization, loop accounting, and dispatch.
- Accepted bot turns use the shared `channels.defaults.botLoopProtection` policy. No Feishu-only loop-control surface is added.
- Automatic text/chunk/card replies deterministically mention the peer bot with the payload-correct Feishu syntax so delivery does not silently stop. Explicit `message_tool` sends remain author-controlled.
- Bot name lookup is bounded by timeout, cache, in-flight deduplication, and a missing-scope circuit breaker.

Required Feishu permissions for this opt-in path are `im:message.group_at_msg.include_bot:readonly` and `im:message:readonly`.

## Why

Feishu can deliver bot-authored group mentions, but app-scoped bot IDs and payload-specific mention syntax make a naive implementation unsafe and unreliable. The final implementation verifies recipient identity at the Feishu transport boundary, keeps shared loop policy in core, and adds no behavior for existing configurations.

## Verification

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/feishu/src/bot.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/bot-name.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/markdown.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/reply-dispatcher.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/bot.stripBotMention.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/config-schema.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/bot.checkBotMentioned.test.ts` — 7 files, 274 tests passed.
- `node --import tsx scripts/generate-bundled-channel-config-metadata.ts --check` — passed.
- `node --import tsx scripts/generate-config-doc-baseline.ts --check` — passed.
- `node scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mjs --check` — passed.
- `node scripts/format-docs.mjs --check` — 718 files clean.
- `node scripts/generate-docs-map.mjs --check` — passed.
- Hosted changed-surface gate: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29569408352 — passed.
- Final rebased branch autoreview — clean, zero findings, confidence 0.95.

## Real behavior proof

Contributor proof used two bots and one human in a live Feishu group. Bot-to-bot exchanges continued across text, chunked, and card replies; the deterministic reply backstop restored a missing model-authored mention; and disabling bot ingress suppressed replies. Identifiers were redacted. The maintainer rework preserves that ingress/reply capability while making it default-off and adding verified recipient identity plus shared loop protection.

## Release note

Feishu accounts can opt into bot-authored group mentions with reliable peer-bot reply mentions and the shared bot-loop guard.

target.title: fix(sqlite): stop mount probes blocking database startup
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

SQLite startup falls back to the system `mount` command when `/proc/self/mountinfo` is unavailable. That synchronous probe had no deadline, so a stalled `mount` process could block state or plugin database initialization indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fallback probe now has a one-second hard timeout. If filesystem classification times out, SQLite conservatively uses rollback journaling instead of assuming WAL is safe. Existing behavior for successful mount classification and non-timeout probe failures is preserved.

## User Impact

Database-backed OpenClaw startup no longer waits indefinitely on a wedged mount probe. When the deadline is reached, startup continues with rollback journaling, avoiding both the hang and an unsafe WAL assumption for an unclassified network filesystem.

## Evidence

- Regression-first tests cover the missing timeout and the conservative timeout policy.
- Before: the production `configureSqliteWalMaintenance` path with an isolated stalled `mount` fixture exceeded a 4-second external guard (`exit_status=124`).
- After: the same production path returned in about 1.0 seconds, selected `journal_mode=delete`, and exited successfully.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.infra.config.ts src/infra/sqlite-wal.test.ts` on Node 24.15.0: 38 tests passed.
- `oxfmt --check src/infra/sqlite-wal.ts src/infra/sqlite-wal.test.ts`: passed.
- Type-aware oxlint and TypeScript checking for the affected files: passed.
- `codex review --base origin/main`: no actionable findings after the conservative rollback follow-up.

Not exercised: a real macOS/BSD host or a real network filesystem. The live proof used the production SQLite configuration call path with a test-only local command fixture.

target.title: fix(e2e): keep phase log tails UTF-8 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`PhaseRunner` (`scripts/e2e/parallels/phase-runner.ts`) keeps a bounded in-memory log tail per phase (`appendTextTail`) and writes that tail to stderr when a phase fails. The bound is applied as a raw byte cut — `Buffer.from(combined).subarray(-tailBytes).toString("utf8")` — so when the retained window starts in the middle of a multi-byte UTF-8 character (emoji/CJK in test output), the diagnostics tail begins with U+FFFD replacement characters.

This is the same bug family as merged #109669 (`scripts/e2e/lib/text-file-utils.mjs`) and open sibling #109670 (`scripts/e2e/parallels/host-server.ts`); `phase-runner.ts` is the remaining byte-based tail decoder in the parallels harness. The three PRs touch separate files and are not stacked; any order merges cleanly.

## Why This Change Was Made

#109669 introduced `decodeUtf8Tail`, which drops leading UTF-8 continuation bytes before decoding a truncated window. This PR exports that helper and reuses it in `appendTextTail`, so the byte cap stays unchanged while the emitted tail always starts on a character boundary. The change is three lines in prod code plus a focused regression test.

Root cause on `main` (`scripts/e2e/parallels/phase-runner.ts:18`): the byte cut from `subarray(-tailBytes)` can start on a UTF-8 continuation byte, and `toString("utf8")` replaces each orphaned continuation byte with U+FFFD.

Deliberately out of scope: `scripts/e2e/parallels/filesystem.ts` has a similar byte-window read, but its only consumer is a regex scan (`extractLastOpenClawVersionFromLog`) whose ASCII pattern cannot straddle a character boundary, so a partial leading character there has no observable effect.

## User Impact

Maintainers reading failed E2E phase output get a clean log tail instead of leading mojibake whenever multibyte text (emoji in test names/output, CJK) crosses the 512 KiB tail cutoff.

## Evidence

Real behavior proof against the production `PhaseRunner` on `main` (driver: construct with a 128-byte cap, `append()` 134 bytes containing an emoji positioned so the byte window starts one byte into it, fail the phase, capture stderr):

Before (origin/main):

```
[phase log tail truncated to last 128 bytes]
���yyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy
contains U+FFFD replacement char: true
```

After (this branch):

```
[phase log tail truncated to last 128 bytes]
yyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy
contains U+FFFD replacement char: false
```

Regression coverage: `test/scripts/parallels-phase-runner.test.ts` drives the real class through a failing phase and asserts the stderr tail (1) contains no U+FFFD when the byte cut splits a character, (2) keeps the full emoji tail when the cut lands on a character boundary, (3) leaves short logs untruncated.

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/parallels-phase-runner.test.ts` — 3/3 pass on this branch; the split-character test fails on unpatched `phase-runner.ts` (control-red verified by reverting the prod file to `origin/main`).
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/e2e-text-file-utils.test.ts` — pass (sibling helper tests unaffected by the new export).
- `oxfmt --check` on all touched files — clean; `oxlint` on touched files — 0 findings; `tsgo --noEmit -p tsconfig.scripts.json` — no errors in touched files (pre-existing `packages/net-policy` errors come from a stale local `ipaddr.js@1.9.1`, unrelated).
- `git diff --check` — clean.

target.title: feat(slack): support running as a real Slack user (user identity)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Today OpenClaw's Slack channel can only run as a Slack **app/bot** — it appears as an app in the member list, is `@mention`-gated, and fundamentally cannot participate in the places people actually talk: a bot can never join a 1:1 DM or an existing group DM. Operators who want an agent that behaves like a real teammate (posts under a human's name, gets DMed, replies in group DMs) have no supported way to do it.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds an opt-in, account-level `identity: "bot" | "user"` mode for the Slack plugin (default `"bot"`, so existing setups are unchanged).

`identity: "user"` authenticates as the authorizing human via a **user OAuth token (`xoxp`)** for all reads and writes, so messages appear under that person's name. A minimal **companion app** carries realtime events subscribed **"on behalf of users"** (Events API, Socket Mode or HTTP) — which is the *only* official mechanism to receive DMs and group DMs, since delivery is scoped to what the authorizing human can see and no bot can be present in those conversations.

We deliberately rejected the browser-session-token (`xoxc`/`xoxd`) "self-bot" approach used by chat bridges: it is unofficial, ToS-grey, session-fragile, and Slack is sunsetting the last legacy realtime path (classic apps end 2026-11-16). The user-token + companion-app path is the officially supported route.

Design notes: one identity-aware `resolveSlackOperationToken` (the duplicated `userTokenReadOnly` gate was removed); the human's own `user_id` (from `auth.test` on the user token) becomes the mention/DM target and the self-send dedupe source, so the agent never replies to its own messages; `@slack/bolt` runs token-less via `token: userToken` (verified against Bolt source). No `xoxc`/`xoxd`, no bot user required.

## User Impact

- Operators can opt a Slack account into acting as a **real person** (`identity: "user"`), including full DM and group-DM participation, with the companion app as invisible plumbing.
- **Existing bot setups are unaffected** — `identity` defaults to `"bot"` and all bot-identity behavior is byte-neutral; no config migration.
- Docs add the exact companion-app recipe (user scopes, on-behalf-of-user event subscriptions, Socket/HTTP config examples) in `docs/channels/slack.md`.

## Evidence

- **Full Slack plugin suite green**: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/slack` → 121 files / 1922 tests passing, confirmed stable across 5 consecutive parallel runs (a shared-state test flake surfaced during review and was fixed — see the final commit).
- **Typecheck**: `tsgo:core` / `tsgo:extensions` / `tsgo:extensions:test` clean (Blacksmith Testbox).
- **Review**: each slice independently reviewed (Codex `gpt-5.6-sol`); the transport's token-less Bolt startup and self-send dedupe were verified directly against `@slack/bolt` source; the token model against Slack's official docs.
- **Behavior-neutral for `identity: "bot"`**: no existing bot-identity assertions changed.

**Known validation gap (intentional, opt-in):** live delivery of bot-less user-scope `message.im`/`message.mpim` events is documented by Slack via the scope/visibility model but is thinly exercised in the wild; end-to-end verification in a live workspace is pending. Because the feature is opt-in and default-`bot`, this does not affect existing users — the live check is a fast-follow, and any Slack-side wrinkle is a documented follow-up rather than a regression.

target.title: fix: reject unsafe Mattermost API path segments
target.body:
Closes #98389

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Mattermost plugin REST calls could reach a different bearer-token endpoint when a dynamic path component contained relative, URL-normalized, or malformed percent-encoded segments.

The affected workflow is Mattermost channel operation through the plugin REST client. Operators expect post, user, and channel ids to select the intended Mattermost endpoint; unsafe path-shaped values should fail before the client attaches the bot token and calls fetch.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Mattermost client now rejects unsafe API path segments at one shared URL-builder boundary before preparing authorization headers. The direct authenticated media-file download path reuses the same builder. The guard handles raw `.` / `..`, encoded dot segments, backslash separator normalization, URL parser TAB/CR/LF normalization, and malformed percent encoding.

Normal Mattermost paths and request bodies are unchanged. This PR does not alter token storage, account resolution, or Mattermost response handling.

## User Impact

Mattermost users and operators get safer fail-closed behavior for malformed or unexpected REST path inputs. Legitimate Mattermost plugin requests continue to use the same `/api/v4` endpoints.

## Evidence

Before/source proof:

- On current `main`, `buildMattermostApiUrl` appended the requested suffix to `/api/v4` without rejecting dot segments first.
- WHATWG URL parsing normalizes examples like `http://localhost:8065/api/v4/posts/../users/me` to `/api/v4/users/me`, so a path-shaped id can change the endpoint selected under the Mattermost bot token.

After-fix proof on this branch:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/client.test.ts extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor-resources.test.ts` — 44 tests passed.
- The media regression supplies raw, encoded, backslash, URL-control, and malformed paths and proves `saveRemoteMedia` receives no request.
- Type-aware targeted oxlint passed for the four touched files.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Fresh uncommitted and full-branch autoreview passes reported no accepted/actionable findings.

No live Mattermost credentials were used. The requested mocked transport proof exercises the production shared URL builder before either authenticated transport boundary.

target.title: fix(promotions): guard JSON.parse against corrupt DB data
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`parseSlugListJson` in the promotions-feed module parses JSON from the `notified_slugs_json` database column without a try-catch. If the DB row is corrupted, `JSON.parse` throws an uncaught SyntaxError that propagates up and gets swallowed by the outer catch handler, silently masking the data corruption instead of gracefully degrading.

## Why This Change Was Made

Same pattern as #109721 and #109754: JSON data from external sources (files, network, database) should be guarded with try-catch to prevent SyntaxError escape.

## Evidence

- The fix wraps `JSON.parse(raw)` in try-catch, returning an empty Set on parse failure — matching the existing behavior for null/empty input
- The outer caller `readPromotionsFeedStateWithMetadata` already has try-catch that returns `EMPTY_STATE` on error, so the degraded behavior is consistent

## Merge Risk

Low. The try-catch returns the same empty Set that null/non-array input already produces.

target.title: fix(heartbeat): remove abort listener on manual stop

## What Problem This Solves

The `cleanup` function in `startHeartbeatRunner` is registered as an abort listener via `addEventListener("abort", cleanup, { once: true })`. It is also returned as `stop` for manual teardown. When called manually via `stop()`, the abort listener was never removed, keeping a stale reference on the `AbortSignal`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Same pattern as #109708 and #109868: exposed cleanup functions that double as abort listeners must detach themselves on manual invocation to prevent listener leaks.

## Evidence

- Existing heartbeat-runner scheduler tests continue to pass (25/28, the 3 timing-related failures are pre-existing flaky tests that also fail on main)
- The fix is a single line addition of `removeEventListener` at the top of `cleanup`, mirroring the established pattern in `channel-runtime-contexts.ts` and `compaction-safety-timeout.ts`

## Merge Risk

Low. The `removeEventListener` call is a no-op if the listener was already auto-removed by `{ once: true }` on abort, and correctly detaches it when `stop()` is called manually.

target.title: fix(infra): bound stalled provider JSON/text/binary response reads with default chunk timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Provider JSON, text, and binary response reads have no per-chunk idle timeout. When a provider sends response headers but stalls mid-body, the `ReadableStream` `reader.read()` call blocks indefinitely, hanging the agent run until the user manually cancels it. The same unbounded read affects the non-2xx error-body path (`readResponseTextLimited` → `extractProviderErrorInfo`), so a provider that returns error headers and then stalls also hangs.

## Why This Change Was Made

`readProviderJsonResponse`, `readProviderTextResponse`, and `readProviderBinaryResponse` each call `readResponseWithLimit` without passing `chunkTimeoutMs`. Inside `readResponsePrefixFromReader`, an absent `chunkTimeoutMs` falls through to bare `reader.read()`, which never times out on its own. The sibling error-body function `readResponseTextLimited` had the same gap—its callers (`extractProviderErrorInfo`, `provider-transport-fetch`) also had unbounded reads.

The fix:

- Adds optional `chunkTimeoutMs`/`timeoutMs`/`onIdleTimeout`/`onTimeout` parameters to all three public response helpers and to `readResponseTextLimited`.
- Sets a **30-second idle default** for JSON and text responses (binary downloads are opt-in since they can be large and callers should choose their own budget).
- Sets a **10-second idle default** for error-body reads via `readResponseTextLimited` (error bodies are small, typically <16 KB, and a shorter timeout means faster recovery from stalled error responses).

This eliminates the entire hang class: both 2xx success paths and 4xx/5xx error paths now have bounded idle reads.

## User Impact

Provider requests that would previously hang the agent forever now fail with an actionable timeout error—within 30 seconds for mid-response stalls and within 10 seconds for stalled error-body reads. Successful responses are unaffected.

## Evidence

### Automated tests

- `pnpm test src/agents/provider-http-errors.test.ts`: **18/18 tests passed** (all 3 new stall tests included).


### Live stall proof — exported helpers with default timeouts (no explicit `chunkTimeoutMs`)

A local TCP server sends partial body data and stalls. The exported helpers are called **without** `chunkTimeoutMs`, exercising the 30 s (JSON/text) and 10 s (error-body) defaults.

```
======================================================================
TEST 1: readProviderJsonResponse(response, 'json-default') WITHOUT chunkTimeoutMs
======================================================================
  TCP server listening on :45805
  Server sends headers + partial JSON body then stalls (no close).
  Default idle timeout: 30,000ms

  ✓ REJECTED after 30.1s
  Error: json-default: response body stalled for 30000ms
  ✓ Error message confirms default 30,000ms timeout was applied

======================================================================
TEST 2: readResponseTextLimited(response) WITHOUT chunkTimeoutMs (error body path)
======================================================================
  TCP server listening on :40609
  Server sends 502 headers + partial error body then stalls.
  Default idle timeout: 10,000ms

  ✓ REJECTED after 10.0s
  Error: error body read stalled for 10000ms
  ✓ Error message confirms default 10,000ms timeout was applied

======================================================================
SUMMARY
======================================================================
  ✓ All default timeout paths verified!
  ✓ readProviderJsonResponse(response, label)            → terminates at 30,000ms
  ✓ readResponseTextLimited(response)                    → terminates at 10,000ms
```

The 30 s default fires in **30.1 s** (per-chunk idle: waits until no data for 30 consecutive seconds). The 10 s error-body default fires in **10.0 s**. Both confirm the default values are correctly wired through the exported helper surface with no caller override.

### Regression tests

All existing size-cap regression tests continue to pass unchanged.

## Additional Notes

This bug was discovered via source-code audit of `readProviderJsonResponse` → `readResponseWithLimit` → `readResponsePrefixFromReader`. The `chunkTimeoutMs` parameter already existed in the underlying machinery (PR #40098) — it simply was not wired through to the public provider response helpers or the error-body reader.

### Risk assessment for the 30s default

- **Idle timeout vs. total timeout**: the 30s default is a *per-chunk* idle timeout, meaning a response that continuously sends data (even slowly) will not trigger it. Only a complete stall between chunks will.
- **Caller scope**: ~80 direct callers of `readProviderJsonResponse` + ~8 of `readProviderTextResponse` + ~35 error-path callers. All were audited; none send requests where a >30s inter-chunk pause is legitimate.
- **Upgrade compatibility**: all new parameters are optional, so existing plugin code compiles and runs unchanged—just with a new idle-failure safety net.
- **Binary/audio/video**: left without a default for now; callers must explicitly opt in with `{ chunkTimeoutMs: ... }`.


### Timeout policy stance

These defaults are **per-chunk idle timeouts**, not total operation timeouts. They live in a separate dimension from the existing provider `timeoutSeconds` (`models.providers.<id>.timeoutSeconds`) and do not shorten configured outer deadlines:

- A provider configured with `timeoutSeconds: 120` whose stream sends data every few seconds will never hit the 30 s idle ceiling.
- The idle timeout only fires when **zero bytes** arrive for 30 consecutive seconds mid-body—a state that indicates a broken connection, not legitimate provider latency.
- Callers that need a longer or shorter idle window pass `chunkTimeoutMs` explicitly; the defaults are a safe fallback for the ~80 callers that today have **no** idle protection at all.

This is consistent with the precedent set in PR #83979 (yujiawei): explicit provider timeout values remain the operator-selected ceiling, but helpers with no configured timeout gain a safety watchdog default. For the error-body path specifically (10 s), the shorter ceiling is intentional: error bodies are small (<16 KB, typically sent in one chunk), and a stalled error-body read delays provider error recovery with no diagnostic benefit.

All new parameters are additive and source/binary-compatible. Existing plugin code compiles unchanged and gains idle-failure protection, or can override via `{ chunkTimeoutMs: ... }`.

## What Problem This Solves

`readProxyErrorData` parses network error response bodies with `JSON.parse(new TextDecoder().decode(bytes))` without try-catch. ## Why This Change Was Made

Same pattern as #109721 and #109754: JSON data from external network sources should be guarded with try-catch to prevent SyntaxError escape and enable graceful degradation.

## Merge Risk

target.title: fix(gateway): ignore invalid handshake timeout env for Gateway calls
target.body:
### What Problem This Solves

`callGateway` treated any non-empty `OPENCLAW_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS` value as an active handshake timeout override when choosing the default wrapper timeout. That included invalid values such as `"0"` or `"abc"`.

The shared preauth timeout resolver already rejects those values and falls back safely, but the Gateway call wrapper only checked whether the env var existed. That made the wrapper timeout policy diverge from the shared timeout contract: an invalid env value could incorrectly extend the default wrapper timeout from `10000ms` to the preauth default of `15000ms`.

### Why This Change Was Made

The Gateway call wrapper should only align its default timeout with a valid preauth handshake override. Invalid env values should behave like no env override, leaving the wrapper at its normal `10000ms` default unless a valid config timeout is present.

This change adds `getPreauthHandshakeTimeoutMsFromEnv()` next to the existing connect-challenge env helper and routes both `resolvePreauthHandshakeTimeoutMs` and `callGateway` through that shared parser. The result is one canonical env contract:

| input                                      | shared preauth env value | call wrapper default |
|--------------------------------------------|--------------------------|----------------------|
| unset                                      | none                     | `10000ms`            |
| `OPENCLAW_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS="0"`        | invalid / ignored        | `10000ms`            |
| `OPENCLAW_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS="abc"`      | invalid / ignored        | `10000ms`            |
| `OPENCLAW_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS="30000"`    | `30000ms`                | `30000ms`            |
| `gateway.handshakeTimeoutMs: 30000` config | `30000ms`                | `30000ms`            |

### User Impact

Users and operators who accidentally set an invalid handshake timeout env value now get the normal Gateway call timeout behavior. Valid positive integer env overrides continue to extend the wrapper timeout as before for slower or loaded hosts.

### Real Behavior Proof

- **Behavior addressed:** invalid `OPENCLAW_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS` values were ignored by the shared resolver but still treated as an active wrapper timeout override by `callGateway`.
- **Real environment:** Linux x86_64, Node 24.13.1, commit `135aa7a002` on branch `fix/gateway-invalid-handshake-env-timeout`.
- **Exact proof before this patch:** a temporary regression test set `OPENCLAW_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS="0"`, called real `callGateway({ method: "health" })` with the silent test Gateway client, advanced fake timers by `10000ms`, and expected `gateway timeout after 10000ms`.
- **Observed result before fix:** the assertion failed because the error message was still empty after `10000ms`.
- **Exact current-behavior confirmation before this patch:** the same temporary test passed when asserting no timeout at `10000ms`, then advancing another `5000ms` and expecting `gateway timeout after 15000ms`.
- **Evidence after fix:** the committed regression test now sets `OPENCLAW_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS="0"` and verifies the wrapper times out at `10000ms`.
- **What was not tested:** a live Gateway process with a real invalid shell env; the focused test exercises the same `callGateway` timeout path with the real timeout resolver and fake timers.

### Tests and Validation

```
$ OPENCLAW_HEAVY_CHECK_LOCK_SCOPE=worktree node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/gateway-client/src/timeouts.test.ts src/gateway/handshake-timeouts.test.ts src/gateway/call.test.ts
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.gateway.config.ts
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.gateway-client.config.ts
[test] passed 2 Vitest shards in 16.46s
```

```
$ git diff --check
EXIT=0
```

Formatting was applied with the existing local formatter binary:

```
$ ./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --write packages/gateway-client/src/timeouts.ts packages/gateway-client/src/timeouts.test.ts src/gateway/handshake-timeouts.ts src/gateway/call.ts src/gateway/call.test.ts
Finished in 382ms on 5 files using 6 threads.
```

One package-level regression assertion added: invalid preauth handshake env values return `undefined` from the shared env helper.

One Gateway call regression assertion added: invalid `OPENCLAW_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS="0"` does not extend the default wrapper timeout past `10000ms`.

### Risk Checklist

- **User-visible behavior:** Yes, only for invalid env values. Invalid `OPENCLAW_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS` no longer extends Gateway call wrapper timeout.
- **Config/env/migration behavior:** Env behavior is touched, but no new env var or config key is added. Valid env values keep existing behavior.
- **Security/auth/secrets/network/tool execution:** No.
- **Plugins/providers/channels/SDK:** No plugin/provider behavior changed. The change is in the private Gateway client timeout helper and Gateway call wrapper.
- **Highest-risk area:** Gateway timeout behavior for callers relying on handshake timeout env/config alignment.
- **Mitigation:** Shared parser keeps env semantics consistent with existing preauth resolver tests; focused Gateway call regression covers the invalid env wrapper timeout path; existing valid env/config alignment tests continue to pass.

Closes: N/A

target.title: fix(anthropic): complete transcript reverse-scan windows across short reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Opening a Claude session transcript in the session catalog can fail with a
`Claude transcript changed while it was being read` error even when the file was
not touched.

`readLocalClaudeTranscriptPage` in `extensions/anthropic/session-catalog.ts`
scans the transcript backwards in fixed windows. Each window was filled with a
single positional `handle.read(chunk, 0, size, position)` that then required
`bytesRead === size`, throwing otherwise. A positional read is allowed to return
fewer bytes than requested, so a benign short read tripped that check and failed
the transcript page with a message implying the file changed. The window is
in-bounds (`position` starts at `requestedEnd ≤ stat.size` and only decrements,
`size = min(chunk, position, …)`), so a short read there is not on its own a
reason to fail the page. The forward metadata scan in the same function already
completes short reads by looping; only this reverse scan threw.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reverse scan now fills each window across as many reads as it takes,
advancing both the buffer offset and the file position each read, so a benign
short read no longer surfaces a "transcript changed" error. A zero-byte read
before the window is filled is premature EOF, so that case still throws the same
error — only benign positive short reads stop failing the page. This is the same
loop the forward scan in this file already uses, and it follows the recently
merged short-read completion work (#108941, #108655, #108253) that had not
reached this plugin path; it is a different surface from #108242, which fills
bounded windows in the core gateway (`src/gateway/session-utils.fs.ts`).

## User Impact

No more spurious "Claude transcript changed while it was being read" failure when
paging Claude session transcripts. A zero-byte read before the window is filled
(premature EOF, consistent with the file being truncated or replaced mid-read)
still surfaces the same error.

## Evidence

Changed files: `extensions/anthropic/session-catalog.ts` (reverse-scan fill
loop) and `extensions/anthropic/session-catalog.test.ts` (two regression tests).

- `pages transcripts identically when every reverse-scan read returns short`:
  drives `readLocalClaudeTranscriptPage` through fault-injected short positional
  reads (each read capped to 4 KiB, so each 128 KiB window is completed across
  dozens of consecutive non-zero short reads) and asserts the paged
  items/order/cursor are identical to a normal read across two pages.
- `still reports a truncated transcript when a reverse-scan read hits EOF
  mid-window`: forces a zero-byte read mid-window and asserts the existing
  premature-EOF error is still raised.
- Before this fix the first test fails at the `bytesRead !== size` throw
  (production short reads cannot be induced deterministically, so mocked fault
  injection is the realistic deterministic proof for this failure class).
- `vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-providers.config.ts
  extensions/anthropic/session-catalog.test.ts`: 27 passed (25 existing + 2 new);
  before the fix: 1 failed | 26 passed. oxfmt and oxlint clean; extensions
  typecheck reports no errors in the changed files.
